evidence: book(): converts form.startsAt to a Date, calls this.scheduling.book(...) and returns present(appointment). This is input mapping plus a call to the service, which is a controller's job.
cancel(): returns present(await this.scheduling.cancel(id, new Date())). The cancellation logic stays in the business service.
addNote(): calls this.notes.write(...) and returns { count: (await this.notes.notesFor(id)).length }. This only shapes the response; no rule is applied.
The file contains no database or repository access and no domain validation or policy logic.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: AppointmentsController only does presentation work. It defines the input form shapes (BookingForm, NoteForm) and turns form fields into service arguments, for example parsing startsAt into a Date. It hands every business operation to the business-layer services (SchedulingService.book/cancel, VisitNotesService.write/notesFor) and formats results through the presenter or a small response object. Nothing in the file does persistence, enforces business rules or validates invariants. In addNote, the count is just the length of the list the service returns, which is shaping the response, not a business rule. Passing new Date() to cancel only supplies the current time at the request boundary; any rule that uses that time stays in the service.
